# Instruments

Every command takes a mesh and prints a compact text block; some also write a
PNG, announced by an `IMAGE:` line. Nothing here needs a coordinate typed by
hand -- each one names what it found, and the name is what you pass on.

    m2c.py [--out DIR] <command> [options]

## `overview`
stage 0+1: normalise, classify, render 4 isometric + 6 orthographic projections
```
m2c.py overview <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--built BUILT` | FreeCAD program built so far. Reported, but NOT drawn: these two renders show one solid each. Use `progress --built` for the comparison |
| `--tile TILE` | size in pixels of each view in the two renders (default 440). Raise it to make small features legible; a bigger picture costs more to read |

## `survey`
stage 2: score XY/YZ/XZ and recommend a section plane
```
m2c.py survey <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |

## `spectrum`
stage 3: candidate offsets along a plane normal
```
m2c.py spectrum <mesh> --plane <XY|YZ|XZ> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--plane {XY\|YZ\|XZ}` | the section plane; the levels are measured along its normal (XY -> Z, YZ -> X, XZ -> Y) |
| `--samples SAMPLES` | how many evenly spaced cuts to take along the normal (default 900); a feature thinner than about two steps produces no level |

## `ortho`
stage 3b: 4 views with the feature levels marked
```
m2c.py ortho <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--plane {XY\|YZ\|XZ}` | the section plane; the levels are measured along its normal (XY -> Z, YZ -> X, XZ -> Y); required except with --frame, which sets it |
| `--offset OFFSET` | optional; omit while still choosing the offset. a level NAME from `ortho` (E0, B3), or mid(B2,B5), or a flat face across the axis (F5), or a number. Naming carries whatever precision the level has; a raw number carries whatever you typed |
| `--tile TILE` | size in pixels of each elevation pane (default 900). Larger spreads closely spaced levels further apart on screen |
| `--samples SAMPLES` | sweep resolution used to locate the feature levels |
| `--built BUILT` | FreeCAD program built so far. Reported, but NOT drawn: these panes render one solid. Use `progress --views ortho` for the comparison |
| `--between BETWEEN` | offset midway between two levels, e.g. --between -11.063,11.063 |
| `--no-boundaries` | draw only the part ends, hiding the prism-boundary rules; use when they crowd the view enough to obscure the geometry |
| `--levels {both\|faces\|sweep}` | where the level table comes from. faces: the flat faces across the axis and the ends of round ones -- exact, and a surface lying across the axis gives no level. sweep: where the area of a stack of cuts changes. both (the default): faces, plus any sweep level no face explains, labelled as such. The default can be set with $MESH2CAD_LEVELS |
| `--frame FRAME` | work across an inclined face or axis: a flat face F# (across its normal), a round face F# or a hole stack C# (across its axis), as `faces` names them. The target is turned by the smallest rotation that lays that direction on X, Y or Z; every level, ring and coordinate is then in that frame, and a sketch is built there and turned back when it is written. Give the same --frame to ortho, section and sketch. --face on an inclined face and --op hole on an inclined stack set it themselves |

## `section`
stage 4: the cut at one offset, as named lines and arcs
```
m2c.py section <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--detail DETAIL` | list every primitive of this ring. A ring of 24 or more primitives otherwise prints its repeats as groups, and caps what fits no repeat at its longest primitives. Repeat the flag for more rings |
| `--plane {XY\|YZ\|XZ}` | the section plane; the levels are measured along its normal (XY -> Z, YZ -> X, XZ -> Y); required except with --meridian, or an inclined --face or --frame, which sets it |
| `--offset OFFSET` | a level NAME from `ortho` (E0, B3), or mid(B2,B5), or a flat face across the axis (F5), or a number. Naming carries whatever precision the level has; a raw number carries whatever you typed |
| `--tol TOL` | fit tolerance in mm; default is derived from the mesh's own sampling density |
| `--grid GRID` | snap coordinates to this grid in mm (e.g. 0.05) |
| `--samples SAMPLES` | sweep resolution used to locate the feature levels |
| `--tile TILE` | size in pixels of each pane of the companion elevation render (default 560) |
| `--between BETWEEN` | offset midway between two levels, e.g. --between -11.063,11.063 |
| `--split SPLIT` | cut the profile at a line: "X=M0" (a level along X), "X=N2" (a node's X), S# (a mirror plane), F# (a flat face across the plane, or a round face's axis in it), H# (a helix axis in it), or "X=0". Give it twice -- each with its own --keep -- to cut at the axis and at a level (a revolve of one stretch of a shaft), or write both with their sides: "X>=M0,Z<=B2" |
| `--keep {+\|-}` | which side of --split to keep (+ by default); one per --split, in the same order |
| `--use USE` | restrict the split to these rings: ring names (R1), primitive names (L1_0) or an array (P0), as --use takes them in sketch |
| `--side {above\|below}` | which prism to measure when the offset lands on a boundary; omit to see both |
| `--built BUILT` | the program built so far: its section at the same cut is drawn over the target's (dashed red), and every region where they differ is listed -- MISSING (target only) and EXTRA (built only), with its area, centre and the target ring it lies on |
| `--fill` | with --built: paint the difference -- green missing, red extra, grey both |
| `--project PROJECT` | project everything between --offset (sketch: --at) and this level onto the plane instead of cutting at one level: the outline of all that material, as named rings. A joggled or bent plate is flat at no level, so a cut shows only part of it; its projection is the whole outline |
| `--law LAW` | fit a designed family -- circle, slot or rounded rectangle -- to the profile at levels between this and the other one named, and say how each of its numbers (centre, half-sizes, corner R) changes: a straight line, or not. A drafted pocket or tray whose corners keep or grow their radius is a rounded rectangle on such lines |
| `--face FACE` | take the profile from a flat face `faces` named (F12) instead of cutting: the face's own outline, at its own level, with holes that go into the material and footprints of things standing on it filled. An inclined face is shown in its own frame (see --frame) |
| `--sharp` | with --face: where a chamfer, a round or a turned end (a face leaning across the outline, not a wall) has cut the face's edge back, carry the walls on either side -- and the walls those faces meet beyond it -- on to their corners instead: the sharp block, to cut the blend from with --op chamfer / --op fillet |
| `--levels {both\|faces\|sweep}` | where the level table comes from. faces: the flat faces across the axis and the ends of round ones -- exact, and a surface lying across the axis gives no level. sweep: where the area of a stack of cuts changes. both (the default): faces, plus any sweep level no face explains, labelled as such. The default can be set with $MESH2CAD_LEVELS |
| `--meridian MERIDIAN` | the profile about an axis at EVERY angle instead of one cut: a round face F# or hole stack C# from `faces` (its axis, which must be X, Y or Z), or a line like Y=0,Z=0. 72 half-plane cuts through the axis give two profiles: the envelope (material at ANY angle -- holes filled, blades and teeth as full rings) and the core (material at EVERY angle -- blades and teeth gone). Use it when a cut through the axis crosses holes, blades or teeth. With sketch: --op revolve --use <its rings> |
| `--frame FRAME` | work across an inclined face or axis: a flat face F# (across its normal), a round face F# or a hole stack C# (across its axis), as `faces` names them. The target is turned by the smallest rotation that lays that direction on X, Y or Z; every level, ring and coordinate is then in that frame, and a sketch is built there and turned back when it is written. Give the same --frame to ortho, section and sketch. --face on an inclined face and --op hole on an inclined stack set it themselves |

## `sketch`
compose a sketch from named primitives and emit one FreeCAD feature
```
m2c.py sketch <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--plane {XY\|YZ\|XZ}` | the section plane; the levels are measured along its normal (XY -> Z, YZ -> X, XZ -> Y); required except with --op hole, whose stack sets its own axis, with --meridian, and with an inclined --face or --frame, which set it |
| `--at AT` | the sketch plane. a level NAME from `ortho` (E0, B3), or mid(B2,B5), or a flat face across the axis (F5), or a number. Naming carries whatever precision the level has; a raw number carries whatever you typed. Not needed with --face |
| `--use USE` | comma-separated primitive names, e.g. 'A0_0,A1_0' or 'A0_0@upper', ring names (R1) or an array (P0). Not needed with --face, or with --split, which takes the whole section unless --use narrows it: the names are the section's (`section --split` prints the kept rings under them), they pick from what the cut keeps, and a hole stays a hole; a hole named alone is a cutter (--combine cut) |
| `--op {extrude\|revolve\|loft\|sweep\|hole\|fillet\|chamfer}` | extrude (default): constant section between --at and --to. revolve: rings or a half profile about --axis. loft: a section that changes between the levels. sweep: a profile carried along --along. hole: a drilled, counterbored or countersunk hole built from the coaxial stacks `faces` names (--use C3 or C3,C4,...): each bore step, countersink, chamfer and drill point as measured, along any axis (an inclined stack is cut in its own frame); cuts, so it takes --base and no --plane/--at/--to. fillet / chamfer: round or bevel a sharp edge of the build into the target's blend face that `faces` names (--use F12 or F12,F13): a fillet is a cylinder (straight edge) or torus (circular edge), a chamfer a narrow plane or cone; cut on a convex edge, added on a concave one (a cove); takes --base and no --plane/--at/--to |
| `--project PROJECT` | project everything between --offset (sketch: --at) and this level onto the plane instead of cutting at one level: the outline of all that material, as named rings. A joggled or bent plate is flat at no level, so a cut shows only part of it; its projection is the whole outline; the profile is that outline, sketched at --at |
| `--law` | with --op loft and one ring in --use: loft between that ring's fitted family (circle, slot, rounded rectangle) at --at and at --to, from the straight lines its numbers follow in between -- not the traced rings. See section --law |
| `--taper` | with --op extrude: a draft. The angle is measured, not typed: the profile at --to must be the one at --at offset by a constant, and the offset over the height is the draft (a drafted pocket, a socket entry, a cast wall). Refused, with by how much, when it is not |
| `--between BETWEEN` | with --op sweep --along H0: the two levels on the helix axis the swept profile runs between (default: the whole part). Any ring is swept -- a thread or worm tooth, not only a round wire -- one turn at a time, patterned by the pitch and trimmed to the levels |
| `--profile PROFILE` | with --split and --op sweep: which kept piece is the profile, as `section --split` names them (a tooth cut off the core at its radius) |
| `--to-profile TO_PROFILE` | the section at the other end of --along W#, as <level>:R#,R#: rings of the section square to the path there (`end` for the level `section` printed at that end of a tube's path). The --use profile is lofted into it along the path, holes as holes; for a pipe that changes shape as it bends. Refused when the two ring sets don't pair |
| `--stations STATIONS` | with --to-profile: sweep through K sections square to the path, the two named ends and K-2 cut from the target between them, each ring resampled to matched points (default 5 when the two ends differ in area, else 2: the ends alone) |
| `--along ALONG` | path for --op sweep: H0, the helix `overview` fitted (H0@body or H0@ends when the end turns are wound tighter than the body; H1, H2 ... on other bodies of the mesh), or W#: a tube's path that `faces` chains from its round faces, or the centreline of the strip ring R# that `section` names (a wire or pipe cut in its own plane). W# is the path last printed under that name, on the plane it was printed on. The profile is --face F# (an end face, holes and all) or --use rings of a section across the path, on any plane, swept from where it meets the path; --use of the strip itself sweeps a round wire of the strip's width |
| `--smooth` | for --op loft: blend the two profiles with curvature instead of straight lines. Use it when the section turns between the levels rather than tapering; a helical gear's tooth costs 2.5 IoU built ruled |
| `--split SPLIT` | cut the profile at a line: "X=M0" (a level along X), "X=N2" (a node's X), S# (a mirror plane), F# (a flat face across the plane, or a round face's axis in it), H# (a helix axis in it), or "X=0". Give it twice -- each with its own --keep -- to cut at the axis and at a level (a revolve of one stretch of a shaft), or write both with their sides: "X>=M0,Z<=B2" |
| `--keep {+\|-}` | which side of --split to keep (+ by default); one per --split, in the same order |
| `--axis AXIS` | revolve axis: a round face's axis (F#), a helix `overview` fitted (H#), a rotation axis `symmetry` names (S#), or two world constraints with levels or numbers, e.g. --axis "Y=mid(B2,E1),Z=E0" or "X=0,Y=0" |
| `--to TO` | where the feature stops: a level NAME (E1, B3, K0, M0, T0), mid(A,B), a flat face across the axis (F5: the level it lies at), or a number. There is no 'boundary' or 'end' keyword: every level has a name, so name the one you mean. For --op loft, a comma-separated list lofts through every level in turn (--to B1,B2,B3), which is what a section that TURNS as it travels needs; two levels can only say it goes from this shape to that one. For --op revolve of rings, a face F#: the revolve turns until the profile is square to it (the flat end face, or the cylinder that carries on from a bend), whichever way round stays inside the part |
| `--angle ANGLE` | revolve angle in degrees (signed: the sense is the right hand about --axis). Rings named with --use and an --axis that crosses none of them -- an annulus about a pipe bend's axis, a half-profile beside the part's axis -- revolve with their holes kept as holes; --to F# ends one without a sign to choose |
| `--tol TOL` | fit tolerance in mm; default is derived from the mesh's own sampling density |
| `--grid GRID` | snap coordinates to this grid in mm (e.g. 0.05) |
| `--samples SAMPLES` | sweep resolution used to resolve level names; keep it equal to the value the names came from |
| `--side {above\|below}` | force a side at a boundary; normally inferred from --use |
| `--base BASE` | a program built so far; the new feature is unioned onto it (or cut from it, see --combine) |
| `--combine {add\|cut\|intersect\|separate}` | with --base: what the new feature does to the program so far. add (default) unions it; cut subtracts it (holes, pockets, slots, a cylinder or sphere seat -- any --op builds the cutter); intersect keeps only what lies inside it (a clipping solid), or with --with N clips feature #N alone; separate keeps it a body of its own beside the rest (a screw in a plate, a bush in a housing, a second part of an assembly), which later features fuse with only where they touch it. The tool is the finished feature, inner rings included; a hole ring named alone in --use is filled to make it |
| `--with WITH_FEATURE` | with --combine intersect: clip feature #N only (as the `program:` line numbers them) and leave the rest alone -- #N becomes #N intersected with the new feature. A joggled plate: the strip from a cut across the bend, then its outline extruded with --combine intersect --with <the strip> |
| `--replace REPLACE` | with --base: the new feature takes the place of feature #N of the base instead of being added after the last one. Every other feature stays as it was. The numbers are the ones each --check prints on its `program:` line |
| `--emit EMIT` | write the program to this path |
| `--check` | execute it and report bbox/volume |
| `--show-program` | print the whole FreeCAD program. It is not printed otherwise; the `feature:` and `program:` lines say what it holds, by the names you work with |
| `--grow GROW` | push named profile edges outward before building, e.g. --grow "L0_3=1.0", so the feature OVERLAPS what it joins instead of sharing a face with it. Per-edge and by name on purpose: growing the whole profile would move dimensions that were measured exactly |
| `--both` | extrude the same distance EITHER SIDE of the sketch plane, for a feature measured at its own mid-thickness |
| `--pattern PATTERN` | repeat the feature N times evenly about a world axis, e.g. --pattern "5@Y=0,Z=0" (use the angles `residual` measured rather than counting them off a picture), or in a row: --pattern "4@B1..B4", the last copy moved by the distance from level B1 to B4 along the sketch axis ("4@X:B1..B4" along another axis). A cut is patterned the same way |
| `--mirror MIRROR` | add the feature's mirror image too: about a mirror plane `symmetry` names (S0), or a level -- M0, any level, mid(A,B) -- on the sketch axis ("Y:M0" on another axis). A cut is mirrored the same way. Build one side of a symmetric part and mirror it |
| `--face FACE` | sketch on a flat face `faces` named (F12): the face is the sketch plane and its outline the profile, and the feature goes into the side the material is on. An inclined face is sketched in its own frame (see --frame): --to then names the levels across it, such as a parallel face |
| `--sharp` | with --face: where a chamfer, a round or a turned end (a face leaning across the outline, not a wall) has cut the face's edge back, carry the walls on either side -- and the walls those faces meet beyond it -- on to their corners instead: the sharp block, to cut the blend from with --op chamfer / --op fillet |
| `--levels {both\|faces\|sweep}` | where the level table comes from. faces: the flat faces across the axis and the ends of round ones -- exact, and a surface lying across the axis gives no level. sweep: where the area of a stack of cuts changes. both (the default): faces, plus any sweep level no face explains, labelled as such. The default can be set with $MESH2CAD_LEVELS |
| `--meridian MERIDIAN` | the profile about an axis at EVERY angle instead of one cut: a round face F# or hole stack C# from `faces` (its axis, which must be X, Y or Z), or a line like Y=0,Z=0. 72 half-plane cuts through the axis give two profiles: the envelope (material at ANY angle -- holes filled, blades and teeth as full rings) and the core (material at EVERY angle -- blades and teeth gone). Use it when a cut through the axis crosses holes, blades or teeth. With sketch: --op revolve --use <its rings> |
| `--frame FRAME` | work across an inclined face or axis: a flat face F# (across its normal), a round face F# or a hole stack C# (across its axis), as `faces` names them. The target is turned by the smallest rotation that lays that direction on X, Y or Z; every level, ring and coordinate is then in that frame, and a sketch is built there and turned back when it is written. Give the same --frame to ortho, section and sketch. --face on an inclined face and --op hole on an inclined stack set it themselves |

## `progress`
the 4 iso views with target and reconstruction superimposed
```
m2c.py progress <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--built BUILT` | FreeCAD program built so far |
| `--tile TILE` | size in pixels of each view (default 680) |
| `--views {iso\|ortho}` | iso (default): the four isometric views; ortho: the four elevations of --plane |
| `--mode {channel\|diff}` | channel: two opaque renders combined by colour channel; diff: translucent build plus boolean difference |
| `--plane {XY\|YZ\|XZ}` | required for --views ortho |

## `edit`
list, drop or undo the features of a program `sketch` wrote
```
m2c.py edit <mesh> --built <built> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--built BUILT` | the program to edit (normally the one you --emit to) |
| `--drop DROP` | remove feature #N; the features after it keep their order and are renumbered. Without --drop or --undo, edit lists the features with each one's own volume and bbox |
| `--undo` | restore the program as it was before its last --emit (every --emit keeps a numbered version; repeated --undo walks further back) |
| `--feature FEATURE` | with --mirror or --pattern: the feature #N (as the list numbers them) to mirror or repeat, a cut too |
| `--mirror MIRROR` | with --feature N: add feature #N's mirror image, about S# from `symmetry` or a level on a named axis, e.g. "Y:M0" |
| `--pattern PATTERN` | with --feature N: repeat feature #N, "5@Y=0,Z=0" about an axis or "4@X:B1..B4" in a row |
| `--emit EMIT` | write the edited program to this path (normally the same path as --built). Without it nothing is saved |
| `--show-program` | print the whole program after --mirror or --pattern |
| `--check` | build the edited program and report bbox, volume, residual and the change against the last saved version |

## `faces`
the planes, cylinders, cones, spheres, tori and revolved splines the mesh was tessellated from, named, with how each pair meets and which directions they carry
*Contributed by mesh2cad (`mesh2cad.contrib.instruments.faces`).*
```
m2c.py faces <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--tol TOL` | how far a vertex may sit off a surface and still be on it, in mm; default is read off the mesh (coplanar neighbours agree to float precision, the rest do not) |
| `--top TOP` | how many surfaces to list, largest first; the rest are counted by kind and all of them are in faces.json |
| `--tile TILE` | size in pixels of each view in the surface render (default 440) |
| `--no-render` | skip the picture; the text and faces.json are unchanged |
| `--cover COVER` | does this surface really run where you think it does? A cylinder F# (axis along X, Y or Z) is continued over --between, or the whole part, and the target's surface on it is measured: the share of that stretch it covers, where, and how far round. A plane F# gives the area on it and its extent. Before building one feature across a stretch, check that its surface spans it |
| `--between BETWEEN` | with --cover: two named levels along the cylinder's axis |

## `residual`
boolean difference against the target, split into named bodies with volume, centre and angle -- the remainder as a work list
*Contributed by Dmitry Zhemchuzhnikov (`mesh2cad.contrib.instruments.residual`).*
```
m2c.py residual <mesh> --built <built> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--built BUILT` | the FreeCAD program built so far |
| `--axis AXIS` | report each body in cylindrical coordinates about this axis, e.g. --axis "Y=0,Z=0"; a circular pattern then reads off the angle column |
| `--min-volume MIN_VOLUME` | ignore bodies below this volume in mm^3; default 0.01% of the target |
| `--tile TILE` | size in pixels of each view in the residual render (default 440) |
| `--solo` | render the residual ON ITS OWN, with neither the target nor the reconstruction alongside it |
| `--views {all\|iso\|ortho}` | which projections to draw |
| `--plane {XY\|YZ\|XZ}` | draw the four elevations in which this plane is edge-on, WITH a scale and the residual's own feature levels marked -- so the extent of each leftover body can be read off and passed to --at |
| `--samples SAMPLES` | sweep resolution used to locate the levels |
| `--frame FRAME` | measure across an inclined face or axis, as section and sketch do: the target and the program are turned into that frame first, so --plane and every position is in it |
| `--export EXPORT` | write the residual to this STL. It then behaves like any other mesh, so `section`, `spectrum` and the rest of the loop can be pointed straight at what is left instead of at the whole part |

## `symmetry`
name the mirror planes and rotation axes, with the --split / --axis flag to pass for each
*Contributed by Dmitry Zhemchuzhnikov (`mesh2cad.contrib.instruments.symmetry`).*
```
m2c.py symmetry <mesh> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--samples SAMPLES` | surface points used to test each candidate |
| `--tol TOL` | distance in mm counted as 'landed back on the surface'; default 0.200% of the bbox diagonal |
| `--top TOP` | how many candidates to name |

## `recall`
print a past command's output again, whole or in part
```
m2c.py recall <command> [options]
```
| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--out OUT` | where to write renders (may go before or after the subcommand) |
| `--grep GREP` | only the lines holding this text |
| `--ring RING` | only this ring of a section, R2 |
| `--lines LINES` | only these lines, a:b |
